posts.body_html:
This clone has me completely FLOORED!
Here's the first pitcher of the season; absolutely phenomenal.


It's extremely tall as well. My 1 inch long rhizome produced this 22 inch tall piker!
For reference, the pot is 3.5 inches wide on each side, and 4 inches tall.


For the time being, I've gagged it with a tissue so no silly wasps will fall inside and chew a hole through the side to escape .

If I remember, I'll check back in a few weeks, see if it retains the pink flush!

Dec 30, 2020 16:29:08 GMT -5 joey said:
I got a batch of AxF seeds from the meadowview charity event thing, they just got out of stratification a few days ago. Really excited to see what they produce in a few months, but I'm gonna hate having to cull any of them
Then don't cull them. I have over 600 seedlings and not culling any until they are at least showing some adult pitchers. Some seedlings that I thought were average turned out to be among the best. Some plants just don't show their true nature until they are older, and by culling them you risk throwing away some beautiful plants. I have seen people here culling 3 months old seedlings because they are not as red, or not as tall. They never even seen the mature pitchers, just tiny thing that are not even pitchers.

Jun 19, 2021 19:27:49 GMT -5 summit said:
Am I missing something? Why was this expected?
This clone opens with a brilliant pink/red flush in the veins and down the body as exhibited in most of the photos in the thread. After several weeks, the color fades to the typical green coloration seen on the usual HCW. You can see this in my latest photo where the pitcher in the foreground is green, and the newest pitcher in the background is red!

The pink/red coloration seems to be inherited from the clone F parent as that plant is known for blushing pink the same way in certain environments (typically cooler regions).

We had our fingers crossed that eventually one division will experience an asexual mutation that causes it to retain the red color throughout the season. Imagine a brilliantly white alba that's always bright red to boot!
